name: currying-partial-application
intent: Specialise a general function by fixing part of its arguments (partial application) or by restating it as a chain of unary functions (currying), so the remaining work is a smaller-arity function value that can be named, passed to higher-order code and called later without threading the bound configuration through every call site.
problem: Code that repeatedly calls the same general function with the same leading arguments - a formatter with its locale, a handler with its repository, a logger with its channel, a comparator with its threshold - scatters that fixed configuration through every call site, or pushes it into globals, wrapper classes or parameter objects that exist only to carry it. Callback-based APIs make it worse: the framework calls you with event data only, so whatever context must not be lost has to be re-attached at every registration. Currying and partial application name the fix: bind the fixed part once, and let the value that travels be a function of the smaller arity.
context: Applies where functions are first-class values and the language has closures or a binding primitive: callbacks and event handlers, higher-order pipelines (map/filter/fold/streams), dependency configuration at composition time (functional core, imperative shell), parsers, formatters and validators with fixed configuration, and DSL or typeclass-style APIs built on unary functions. It is the wrong tool where default, named or keyword arguments already express the specialisation at the call site, where a parameter object documents the fixed values better than a chain of bindings, or where the bound values are mutable and shared.
benefits: Specialisation without boilerplate: one general function yields as many focused functions as needed, and callers see the reduced arity instead of the full parameter list.

Configuration travels inside the value: callbacks, dependency wiring and higher-order pipelines receive a plain function, so no globals, context structs or configuration classes are needed to carry the bound arguments.
The specialised function is a first-class artifact: it can be named, documented, unit-tested and reused, unlike configuration repeated at each call site.

Arity reduction is what higher-order APIs actually ask for: map, filter, andThen, thread pools and event buses want a unary or reduced-arity function, which partial application produces without an adapter class.
Order and naming become explicit decisions: the general function stays neutral while each specialisation states its intent where it is created.
It reuses the language's own function abstraction - closures, bind, curry, method values, placeholder syntax - instead of introducing a new type, framework or base class.
tradeoffs: Partial application binds the leading arguments: when the general function's parameter order does not put configuration first, every specialisation needs a wrapper or an argument flip - the data-last convention that curried libraries impose exists to paper over exactly this.

Each specialisation is a closure or partial object built at runtime: created inside a loop or per request it allocates and adds a call frame, so the pattern carries a usage discipline (hoist it) rather than only a definition.

Diagnostics get worse: specialised functions are anonymous by construction (functools.partial has no __name__, JavaScript reports a bound function as "bound <name>"), so stack traces, profilers and log lines stop naming the operation unless the specialisation is stored under a real name.

Captured values are references: binding a mutable container or a receiver makes the specialised function observe later mutations and turns it into shared mutable state across threads, and in garbage-collected languages it keeps the captured objects alive for as long as the value is stored.

Two related concepts share one label: currying (the f(a)(b) call protocol) and partial application (binding values) are routinely conflated, so a codebase that mixes the protocols - or mixes auto-curried library functions with data-first helpers - produces call sites that cannot be read without looking up the definition.

Curried types erode the type surface: nested function types (A -> B -> C), boxed primitive Function chains and FnOnce restrictions are harder to read and annotate than a named parameter object, and mainstream type systems lose fidelity on the way - TypeScript's bind cannot model generic functions or overloads at all.

In languages with default, named or keyword arguments the call-site motivation disappears and shipping both styles doubles the API surface; and a curried API cannot gain a parameter without breaking every call site that already committed to the chain.

Runtime overhead: each curried call creates an intermediate closure. In tight loops or high-throughput services this allocation and extra call-stack depth can measurably degrade performance - a tuple-style function eliminates this overhead in performance-critical paths.

participants.responsibility: The n-ary function being specialised; the reusable source of behaviour, which must not be edited to add a specialisation.
The values fixed at specialisation time - configuration, dependency, receiver; they must be immutable or deliberately shared, because the specialised value keeps referring to them.
The mechanism that performs the specialisation (closure capture, curry/bind/partial call, method value, placeholder expression) and returns the reduced function.
The resulting smaller-arity function value: the thing that is named, stored, passed around and called later.
The code that accepts the specialised value - callback registration, map/filter/stream operator, dependency container, handler table - and supplies only the arguments that are still missing.
The caller that provides the unbound arguments; for curried chains it must respect the one-argument-per-call protocol.

use_cases: Configuring callbacks: bind tenant, request or connection context once and register a handler that the framework calls with event data only (Function.prototype.bind, Go method values, Java lambdas, C# delegates).
Dependency configuration at composition time: bind a repository, clock or logger to a pure function so the core logic keeps a unary signature (functional core, imperative shell).
Formatter, parser and validator families: derive format_eur, parse_de or is_over(threshold) from one general function and reuse them in tests and in map/filter pipelines.
Handler and route tables: build the concrete handler for a route, command id or message type once, store it in a registry, and let dispatch pass only the payload.
Higher-order pipeline assembly: turn a two-argument comparator or reducer into the unary shape required by sort, map, fold and stream operators without writing a wrapper class.
Test helpers: specialise assertions, predicates and reference factories once per test module instead of repeating the same arguments at every call site.

Redux store wiring: react-redux's `connect` is curried, allowing `connect(mapStateToProps)(MyComponent)` so that mapStateToProps and mapDispatchToProps can be supplied independently across many components without repeating the store connection boilerplate.

Ramda / Lodash-fp pipelines: `R.curry`-decorated functions and `_.curry` from Lodash enable partial application at any argument position via placeholders (e.g. `R.__`), and the resulting unary bindings slot directly into `R.pipe` / `R.compose` / `_.flow` pipelines.
React event handler specialisation: curry a form-submission handler to pre-bind the `onFormSubmit` callback and the event.preventDefault() call, keeping the JSX prop clean.

API client configuration: partial-apply a base URL, auth token or version string to a generic `fetch` function, producing a typed `apiGet` that only needs the path and query parameters at each call site.
Internationalisation formatters: curry a `format(locale, currency, amount)` function to produce `formatUSD`, `formatEUR` helpers that flow directly into a `map` over a list of transactions.

Haskell's default calling convention: every n-ary function is a unary chain (`add :: Int -> Int -> Int`), so `inc = add 1` and operator sections like `map (+3)` are ordinary partial application throughout the language and its standard libraries.

Python callbacks and deferred work: `functools.partial` freezes leading positional and keyword arguments (`basetwo = partial(int, base=2)`) into a callable object that executors, GUI command slots and test helpers store and invoke later with only the remaining arguments.

C++ callback wiring with `std::bind_front` / `absl::bind_front`: the Google/Abseil-prescribed replacement for `std::bind` — fix the leading arguments of a callable once at registration (thread pool task, event-loop handler) and let the host invoke the remaining call.
avoid_when: The language offers default, named or keyword arguments and the specialisation happens only at a call site - use those instead of returning a function.
The fixed values are mutable and shared: pass them explicitly or copy them, instead of freezing a live reference into a closure.
Several values always travel together: a parameter object or context struct documents the group better than a chain of bindings.
The specialised value must satisfy a multi-method interface or a class contract: partial application produces only a callable; write an adapter or strategy object instead.
It is a single call site or a one-off: a named wrapper function - or simply calling the general function - reads better than a binder expression.
The result must be serialised, sent across a process boundary or stored on a durable queue: closures and partial objects are not data.

The function is called millions of times per second in a hot path: the closure allocation overhead per partial application is measurable in CPU-sensitive code; a tuple-based function signature eliminates this cost.

Exposing a public SDK to third-party consumers: a nested `P1 -> P2 -> ... -> R` type signature hides the parameter names and expected shape compared to a flat `(P1, P2) -> R` tuple-style declaration, leading to higher misuse rates.
anti_patterns: Curry-everything APIs: shipping every function as a tower of unary calls so callers cannot read the signature and parameter names disappear from the documentation.

Silent protocol mixing: curried and uncurried overloads of the same name, or auto-curried data-last library functions next to data-first helpers, so arguments end up in the wrong slots without a type error.
Binding mutable state into a closure and passing it off as a pure function, hiding shared mutable state and its concurrency problems behind a small arity.
Per-iteration rebinding: allocating a fresh specialisation inside a hot loop or per request when the same bound function could be hoisted to construction time.
Renaming by binding: wrapping a general function in a partial application only to give it a domain name, when a named wrapper or re-export would be clearer and cheaper.
Hardcoding configuration in hot paths: applying partial application inside a loop called millions of times per second, where the allocation and call-stack overhead of closures becomes measurable.
Exposing curried signatures in public SDKs: forcing third-party callers to understand nested unary chains when a flat tuple-style signature would be clearer and less error-prone.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the general behaviour and the environment it runs in are separate concerns; the specialisation is a value, not a subclass, a flag or a copy of the function.
Dependency inversion: the specialised function carries the concrete dependency, so the consumer depends on the narrowest contract it actually needs.
Interface segregation by arity: consumers receive exactly the parameters they are responsible for, not the whole configuration of the underlying operation.
Open/closed principle: new specialisations are new values derived from the general function; the general function is not edited to add a variant.
Immutability discipline: safe specialisation assumes the bound values do not change, which is what keeps the derived function referentially transparent.
Data-last convention: when designing for composition, put the data parameter last so that curried helpers slot cleanly into pipelines without argument-flipping.
best_practices: Order the general function's parameters so that configuration is bound first, or adopt a data-last convention for the whole codebase, and document that order where the function is declared.
Name the specialised value at module scope; reserve inline binder expressions for trivial adapters used at a single call site.
Hoist specialisation out of loops and request handlers: build the bound function once and pass the value around.

Prefer the language's dedicated primitive (functools.partial, Function.prototype.bind, Proc#curry, std::bind_front, method values) when introspection, signature metadata or framework support matters; use a plain closure when type inference or extra logic matters more.
Keep bound values immutable or copy them; never bind a container whose later mutation would quietly change what the function means.

Test the specialisation as a value, including its remaining arity - the too-few and too-many-argument behaviour differs per language (Ruby's curry raises ArgumentError, JavaScript's bind ignores extra arguments).
Do not rely on fn.length for arity detection when functions have default parameters or rest parameters; pass arity explicitly to curryN-style helpers.
Avoid over-currying: chains beyond three levels (f(a)(b)(c)) typically signal that a parameter object or plain function would be clearer.

In performance-critical code, profile the allocation cost of closure creation per iteration before shipping curried helpers in hot paths; prefer tuple-style signatures when the overhead is measurable.
When mixing curried library functions (Ramda, Lodash-fp) with non-curried utilities, add an explicit comment at the call site if argument order is non-obvious.
Use placeholder syntax (R.__, _.placeholder) when you need to bind a non-leading argument, rather than creating an argument-flip wrapper.
Store each named specialisation under a descriptive variable at module level so that stack traces, profilers and log output retain the semantic name.
